name: Mind maps
summary: From the first sketch to a set of notes or a manuscript: how to change the structure of a map, carry on with the work on another device and pass the result on.
lead:
A mind map rarely stays the way it started. First it is a few notes, then groups and links appear, and later a set of notes, a project plan or a manuscript has to be assembled out of them. The app is useful as long as it lets the structure change as freely as the thinking develops.

So the whole path of the material matters here: a thought has to be written down quickly, then rearranged, and finally used beyond the canvas. Lecture notes and the plan of a novel share a foundation but have different continuations. That is exactly where the specialization of a new editor is worth looking for.

audiences.title: Getting to grips with a complex subject
audiences.body: A student or a reader assembles notes out of concepts, examples and links. Later they need to find a detail and reconstruct the line of the explanation, not just look at a handsome tree.

audiences.title: Sketching and rearranging thoughts
audiences.body: During a lecture or a brainstorm a person writes with the keyboard or with a stylus. A pause to hunt for a command gets in the way of holding on to the next thought.

audiences.title: Preparing material for someone else
audiences.body: The author turns the map into a plan, a manuscript or a document to discuss. The recipient needs to understand the links and read the attachments without installing the same editor.

sections.title: Write it down first, make sense of it after
sections.intro: A good editor allows for things being unclear at the start. The structure gets sharper as the work goes on.

observations.title: Writing at the pace of thought
passages: When sketching out thoughts, a single gesture can be fast, but constantly switching from the keyboard to touch breaks the sequence. What a user needs is a connected set of commands: create a node, move to its neighbor, open a branch and carry on with the text. Keyboard support has to cover that whole path.

A few hotkeys do not yet make it possible to work without the screen. If you can create a node but cannot move to its neighbor or come back out of a branch, the flow is broken all the same. The value of a keyboard mode shows in an ordinary sketch: write down five thoughts, correct the third and carry on from the fifth.

A stylus has a different problem: writing, selecting and moving can conflict. An attempt to write a thought into a node shifts the node, and the author has to watch the gesture instead of the content. Input like that needs controls of its own; moving the keyboard commands onto buttons at the edge of the screen is no substitute.

quotes.text: SimpleMind you are good. You have a lot going for you. But you are not as good as my beloved iThoughts yet. You lack the simple keyboard navigation to expand and condense nodes (or topics), and you lack the keyboard based resizing of the map to zoom in and out with ease.

I really thought this was going to be the app! Unless I'm mistaken though, there are no keyboard shortcuts? To quickly brainstorm, I have to be able to mind map without touching the screen. If there aren't keyboard shortcuts implemented, I can't really use it.
In trying to use my Apple Pencil for text input it caused nodes to drag, to disappear, or didn't actually write. I'm going to try to find an alternative.

placements.title: Writing at the pace of thought

observations.title: Showing a link between different branches
passages: A tree shows belonging: a subject consists of parts. But a historical line, a book or a system can contain a link between elements of different branches. If marking it means duplicating a node, one thought starts living in several places and the map is harder to keep whole.

A link between branches lets you leave the thought in one place and point to it from another. A character, for instance, belongs to one story line but affects an event in another. A label on the relationship explains this to the reader better than another copy of the node does.

Having several types of link should have a reason. One arrow might mean the order of events, another the influence of a character. A filter by relationship helps you read a map like that without deleting part of the material. Color on its own does not explain the meaning of a link to a new reader.

quotes.text: I was looking for a mind map app that showed for non hierarchical relationships (so not just parent-child) and that didn't require a subscription and this has proved to be excellent. App is very fast, and good for taking notes on books, timelines of history, plotting out systems.

Its a very good mind mapping piece of software. I feel you've got a lot of control over how the data is presented, and its much better than many other min map software for linking nodes/elements together.

placements.title: Showing a link between different branches

observations.title: Rearranging the map while keeping the links
passages: Rearranging is the main work with a map, not a repair for a bad start. As the subject becomes clearer, you want to move several related branches together. Moving one node at a time and unpredictable snapping turn a thinking task into tidying up space by hand.

What is needed is a controllable selection of a group and a clear sense of where it will land. It matters to keep free movement around the canvas apart from a change in which branch something belongs to: the same gesture should not quietly change the meaning of the structure. A good editor lets you try a new order and go back without creating the material again.

For the plan of a personal project, rearranging has one more meaning: an order of actions emerges out of a list of concerns. A due date and a completion mark can live right inside the nodes, while a dependency stays visible. That is one possible direction for an editor for personal tasks; the complaints about dragging do not on their own prove that the user needs a new planner.

quotes.text: When you move blocks, the motion is jittery and it snaps to the most random places

Please consider following suggestion: include an option to multi-select branches, sub-branches to be able to move items around. It is very frustrating to spend much time rearranging out of place branches.
Cannot organize and move freely mindmaps the way I want and need to.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Rearranging a map without losing the links”.

placements.title: Rearranging the map while keeping the links

observations.title: Looking at the same material differently
passages: A template helps you start while the structure has not been put into words yet. Once it is filled in, it may turn out that the material is easier to read as a plan or laid out another way. If changing the form is only available on an empty map, the first choice locks in the rest of the work too early.

The content of a map and its appearance are better kept apart. Then a map that has been filled in can be rearranged with the nodes and links intact. A person needs to see what changes when they switch: a linear plan shows the order of reading, a map shows the groups and the relationships between them.

In a study map a branch can be hidden for a while and reconstructed from memory. In a manuscript the scenes can be read one after another. These modes use what has already been written; a separate copy quickly drifts away from the main map and creates extra work checking one against the other.

quotes.text: The templates are helpful tools, and it is also very simple to create your own maps.
My biggest complaints are: Couldn't find the way to switch the template in existing map
There is no option for converting an existing mind map to outline format

placements.title: Looking at the same material differently

sections.title: Carry on wherever it suits you
sections.intro: Changing device should not turn into moving the project by hand or hunting for edits that have gone missing.

observations.title: Opening the latest version on another device
passages: Apps on several platforms solve only part of the problem. What a person needs is the same map with the latest edits when they move from the tablet at home to the computer at work. Uploading and downloading by hand can be acceptable if the need for it is clear in advance.

Working without a network does not necessarily get in the way of carrying on. What matters more is that after reconnecting it is visible that the edits from the tablet have gone through and that this is the version opening on the computer. A saved indicator should describe the real state of the map, not just the presence of an account.

When instead you have to upload the file to a third-party service by hand, a person ends up keeping track of the versions themselves. Carrying on automatically only takes that work away together with a history of changes: if two devices edited the same branch, the earlier variants are needed for a meaningful choice rather than a quiet overwrite.

quotes.text: I'm relatively new to mind mapping and didn't want to try the other versions because of either their lack of cross-platform support or subscription model. I purchased this app for macOS, iPadOS, and windows. It works similarly and equally well on each.
The offline mode seems to work with pretty good syncing once back online

There is no syncing feature in this app, and I'm not sure why. It seems with the ability to collaborate on a mind map, I should also be able to seamlessly work on a map on my iPad, then when I get home, be able to work on it on my desktop without needing to manually upload then download using a 3rd

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Opening the latest version on another device”.

placements.title: Opening the latest version on another device

observations.title: Doing the whole job on the tablet
passages: A tablet can be the main workplace, not a screen for looking at the result. So the presence of a mobile app says little about whether you can rearrange a map, manage the links or carry out a familiar operation with a stylus. A user judges a specific piece of work in a specific interface.

An incomplete set of actions on the tablet is most noticeable in the middle of a project. The map can already be opened, but putting it in order or changing a link has to happen on the computer. So the mobile version is worth judging on a map that has been filled in, and the differences between devices are worth showing before the work starts.

There is another boundary: an app can technically work on a tablet and still be unavailable to a personal account. For an author working alone that is the loss of a workplace, not a detail in a pricing table. A full tablet editor has to explain both the ways of controlling it and the terms of individual access.

quotes.text: The iOS Ayoa application is not ready primetime use. No clear way to clean up a Map. Navigation with the Apple Pencil is poor. Most of the menu options available in the web application are not available.
Often more frustrating to use than helpful. You can't do half of what you can on the web version or it is at least very unclear how to
I've been using Lucid for years and constraining tablets and mobile now to teams/organization and removing the application from supporting individual (paid) account was a terrible decision.

placements.title: Doing the whole job on the tablet

sections.title: Passing on the map along with its meaning
sections.intro: The result can become a document, a presentation or material for revision. It matters to understand that exit in advance.

observations.title: Checking the result through the recipient’s eyes
passages: A finished file is needed so that another person can read the map or use it in their own work. An export completing successfully does not show whether the images, the captions and the structure survived. The format is worth choosing by what the result is for, not by the number of extensions on offer.

Open the export outside the editor and check a meaningful fragment: the text, an embedded picture and a link between branches. If an image will not do, a different format may solve the problem, but that route has to be clear. A recipient is not obliged to own the original app to recover the meaning of what was sent.

For a large map the scale matters: the captions can survive in the file and still be unreadable on the page. A preview of the pagination, the margins and the order of the parts lets you fix the result before sending. For further editing, a suitable format has to be chosen separately.

quotes.text: Exporting as a jpg or a png fails to load, like the file is corrupted. I did have success with a PDF export, though.
I paid for export capability and the image export only gives a 500 internal server error.
I've been testing your app for about a week now and I'm having issues with sharing my map.. Sending it as a pdf in an email doesn't send the included pictures in a box.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Checking the result through the recipient’s eyes”.

placements.title: Checking the result through the recipient’s eyes

conclusion.title: Start with one continuation of the map
conclusion.body:
For a new product I would pick one job that comes after the sketch: turning a study map into material for revision, for example. That makes it possible to test a concrete benefit without building an editor for everyone at once. A student creates a small set of notes, comes back to it a few days later and tries to recall a branch that has been closed. What matters is seeing whether the map helps them get to grips with the subject and whether they add to it willingly.

But input, rearranging and saving have to work first. Without them, self-testing will only complicate a weak editor. For the author of a manuscript the priority would be different — tying the scenes to a linear plan. These directions make more sense to test separately than to unite under a single promise of “thinking better”.
